title: Clipboard Data
summary: Clipboard data collection is the theft of whatever the user last copied, read straight from the operating system clipboard buffer rather than from a file or a database. On Windows this can be as trivial as running the built in clip.exe or calling Get-Clipboard from a PowerShell session, and macOS and Linux offer equivalents such as pbpaste. The behaviour leaves almost no artefact of its own, because no file is created and the buffer is already shared with every process running as that user. Detection therefore rests on process ancestry, on a command line that names a clipboard reader, on the parent that launched it, and on timing relative to the user's own copy action. The same access is used legitimately by password managers and form fillers, so clipboard reads have to be judged by who is reading, under which account, and how often.

beginner.definition: The clipboard is a small area of memory where the computer keeps the last thing you copied. Clipboard data collection means an attacker reads that area to steal what the user copied. It often catches passwords, card numbers or text from a private document.
beginner.whyItMatters: People copy sensitive things all day long at work. They may copy a password from a password manager or an account number from a spreadsheet. Those copies sit in one shared place that many programs can read. An attacker does not need to break any encryption to take them. It is a cheap way to steal credentials on a machine that is already compromised.
howItWorks: The user copies text in any program, and the operating system stores it in a shared clipboard buffer.
Malware running as the same user asks the operating system for the current clipboard contents.
On Windows the attacker may simply run the built in clip.exe tool or the Get-Clipboard command.
On macOS and Linux, tools such as pbpaste read the same buffer and print it for the attacker.
The stolen text is written to a file or sent to a server that the attacker controls.
Some malware also replaces the clipboard content, for example swapping a payment address for one of its own.
beginner.example: Picture an office with one shared whiteboard by the door. Whatever anyone writes there is visible to everyone who walks past. Most of the time it holds a shopping list. Sometimes a colleague scribbles a door code on it before going to lunch. An attacker in the building does not need to break into any office. They just read the whiteboard at the right moment and walk away with the code.
takeaways: The clipboard is shared, so any program running as you can read what you copied.
Reading the clipboard is a normal action, so context decides whether it is malicious.
Clearing the clipboard after copying a password shortens the time it can be stolen.

objectives: Explain what the clipboard is and why many programs are able to read it.
Describe how clip.exe, Get-Clipboard and pbpaste are used to read clipboard contents.
Explain why clipboard access on its own is not proof of malicious activity.
Identify process and command line evidence that points to clipboard theft.
Describe how clipboard content can be replaced to mislead a user.
